privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lead: Short version: this site has no accounts and asks you for nothing. It counts which pages get opened, in which language, and which government documents people click through to. That tells us whether the site is reaching people outside the cities. It never records what you search for. It sets no cookies. And you can switch the counting off at the bottom of this page.

measure.title: What we measure
measure.p1: Which pages get opened, in which of the six languages, and roughly where from. That means your country, and usually your state or city. Also what kind of device you are on and how fast your connection is. There is one reason for all of it: to know how many people this platform reaches, and whether it reaches anyone beyond the big cities.
measure.p2: What you open. A district on the map, a project, the tenders tab, a chart. And which government sources you click through to. The promise of this site is that every figure links back to a government document. Counting which documents people actually open is how we decide which portal to add next. Without that we would be guessing.
measure.p3: Where the site behaves badly. How fast pages load on your device, whether a section failed, whether a page had nothing to show you. These are our own faults, and we would rather measure them where they happen than guess at them on a developer's laptop. Automated crawlers get filtered out before any of this is counted.

never.title: What we never measure
never.p1: What you search for. The search box records that a search happened and whether it found anything. It never records the words. On a site about Andhra Pradesh politics, the words a reader types are the most sensitive thing they produce here. They are stripped out of the web address before anything is recorded, and they are never sent anywhere.
never.p2: Anything that identifies you. There is no account, no login, no name, no email address, no phone number, no user ID, no advertising identifier. Nothing you write into a correction or a message to us gets measured.
never.p3: Because nothing is stored on your device to identify you, what reaches us are counts, not people. We could not pick your visit out of the reports. There is nothing measured here that could be used to contact you or to build a picture of you.

cookies.title: Cookies
cookies.p1: This site sets no analytics cookies. Google Analytics runs here with storage consent permanently denied, which means it counts without writing a cookie and without keeping a lasting identifier for you. That is also why no cookie banner stands in your way. There is nothing to consent to.
cookies.p2: Two small things are kept inside your own browser and never sent anywhere. One is the language you chose, so the site opens in it next time. The other is the fact that you asked not to be counted, and that one is only saved if you use the switch below. Clearing your browsing data removes both.

google.title: Who else sees it
google.p1: The counting is done by Google Analytics 4. Google acts as our processor: it receives the events described above and gives us summary reports. No one else receives those events. We do not sell them, share them or trade them, and there is no advertising on this site.
google.p2: Google uses your IP address briefly, to work out an approximate location and to filter out spam traffic, and then throws it away. Google says it never links raw IP addresses to user identifiers and discards them after use. We never see it, and the site asks Google to shorten it in any case.
google.p3: Google deletes the detailed event records after two months. What survives is aggregate. How many people opened the Projects page in a given month, for example, with nothing underneath it about individuals.
google.p4: Two other Google services are already part of this site, and they are worth naming plainly. The fonts your language needs come from Google Fonts, and a few images are served from Google's image hosting. Loading either one tells Google your IP address and which page asked for it, whether or not you switch the counting off. That is true of every site that uses them. Switching the counting off stops the analytics. It does not stop the fonts.

children.title: Children
children.p1: This site collects no personal information from anyone, at any age, and it has no accounts. So there is nothing here that would treat a student's visit differently from anyone else's. School and college students are among the readers this platform is most for.

changes.title: If this changes
changes.p1: This page describes what the code actually does. It gets updated in the same change as the code, not afterwards. The date at the top is the date it last changed. If anything here is unclear, or looks wrong to you, tell us. Being wrong about our own data handling would be the most serious mistake this platform could make.

choice.title: Your choice
choice.lead: You can switch the counting off for this browser. It takes effect the moment you press it, and nothing further gets sent. On your next visit the analytics script is not loaded at all. Fonts and images are a separate matter, described above.
choice.gpc: Your browser is sending a Global Privacy Control signal, so counting is already switched off for you. Nothing further is needed, and the analytics script has not been loaded on this visit.
choice.noStorage: Counting is off for now. But your browser is blocking site storage, so this choice cannot be remembered. You will need to set it again on your next visit.
choice.scope: This is remembered in this browser only. Another browser, another device, or clearing your browsing data will each need the switch set again. That is a direct result of us not keeping an identifier for you, and we think it is the better trade.

finances.title: State Finances — the debt record
finances.intro: When a family takes a loan, there is one passbook. A state has several: the government's own budget books, the national auditor's (CAG) audited accounts, and the Reserve Bank's records. **They do not always say the same number — so this page shows all of them, side by side, for every year since Andhra Pradesh was divided in June 2014.** Where they disagree, you see the disagreement. Nothing here is our estimate; every figure links back to the document it came from.
finances.threeGovernments: Since bifurcation, AP has had three governments: **TDP (Chandrababu Naidu) Jun 2014 – May 2019**, **YSRCP (Jagan Mohan Reddy) May 2019 – Jun 2024**, and **TDP-led NDA (Chandrababu Naidu) since Jun 2024**.

debt.title: How much does Andhra Pradesh owe?
debt.sub: Outstanding liabilities at the end of each financial year, ₹ crore — three official sources side by side.
debt.provenance: RBI: State Finances — A Study of Budgets 2025-26 (Statement 19). AP: FRBM Statements of Fiscal Policy, apfinance.gov.in. CAG: State Finances Audit Reports for AP. Exact documents listed at the bottom of the page.
debt.body: Read it simply: the debt roughly **doubled between 2015 and 2019** (about ₹1.2–1.5 to ₹2.6 lakh crore, depending on whose book you read), and **nearly doubled again by 2024** (to about ₹4.9 lakh crore). The three sources usually differ by a few thousand crore; for 2016–17 the RBI series differs sharply from the state's books — both are shown exactly as published. CAG's audited series stops at March 2023 because its next report was not yet public.

composition.internalDesc: mostly market bonds investors buy, plus bank/NABARD loans, NSSF, UDAY bonds

offBudget.title: The debt outside the books
offBudget.sub: Borrowings taken through state corporations — CAG says these are NOT included in the headline debt above.
offBudget.provenance: CAG State Finances Audit Reports FY2020–FY2023; FY2024 figure attributed to the Principal AG in a Feb 2026 Legislative Council reply (secondary source, labeled).
offBudget.body: In CAG's own words, these borrowings "do not find mention in the Finance Accounts" and stayed "outside legislative control". They grew from **₹26,097 crore (March 2020)** to **₹1,28,048 crore (March 2023)** — and CAG states that counting them takes the real debt burden to **41.89% of the state's economy** in 2022-23, against ~33% without them. This is why two people quoting "the debt" can both point at official numbers and still differ by a lakh crore.

guarantees.title: Guarantees — promises to repay someone else's loan
guarantees.sub: If a state corporation cannot repay, the government must. Outstanding guarantees, ₹ crore.
guarantees.provenance: RBI Statement 28 (compiled from state governments and CAG); 2025-26 figures from AP's FRBM books, labeled.
guarantees.body: Guarantees were under ₹11,000 crore in 2015 and crossed **₹1.5 lakh crore by 2024** — a 14-fold rise across both governments. A guarantee is not yet debt, but it becomes debt the day the corporation fails to pay.

ratio.body: Around **23%** in 2015, around **35%** now — and remember, this line does NOT include the off-budget borrowings above. The commonly cited FRBM guideline for states is far below today's level.

a.perGovernment: Debt grew under all three. Each figure below is the increase between the March before a government took office and the March after it left, taken from one source family at a time so the comparison stays like-for-like.
a.threeSources: All three. The Reserve Bank, Andhra Pradesh's own budget books and the national auditor each publish a total for the same 31 March, and they differ because they count different things. Two people can quote official figures and still disagree — that is not a trick, it is how the record is kept.
a.composition: Mostly bonds sold to banks and investors. But a large part is money the government is holding rather than money it went out and borrowed — its own employees' provident fund, deposits and reserve funds, all of which it owes back.
a.hidden: Two things. Loans taken through government corporations, which the state has to repay but which never appear in the main debt number. And guarantees, which are not debt until the borrower fails to pay — and then they are.
a.tooBig: That depends on the economy it sits against. This compares the debt to everything Andhra Pradesh produces in a year, the way a bank compares a loan to an income rather than looking at the loan alone.
a.deficits: No, and it has not in any year since bifurcation. A fiscal deficit means the state spent more than it earned. A revenue deficit is the harder one: it means the state borrowed to cover salaries, pensions and interest, before building anything at all.
a.departments: A state-wide total cannot tell you whether money went into school buildings or anywhere else. The Demands for Grants can, because the budget is voted department by department, every year.
a.claims: Each incoming government has published a white paper about the one before it. These are political documents, not audits. We show what each claimed beside what the audited record says, and leave the comparison to you.

The state spent **{bestPct}%** of its voted capital money in {bestFy}. promised.seriesBody: The fall does not begin at a change of government. Voted capital spending drops from 83.5% in 2015-16 to 43.2% in 2017-18 under the same government, and no year since has reached half. Over the same period the amount voted roughly quadrupled, from ₹11,227 crore to ₹45,344 crore. The announcements grew; the delivery did not.

why.p1: Everything a citizen of Andhra Pradesh might want to know about their government's work is already published somewhere — a tender on one portal, the sanction order on a second, the budget release on a third, the audit report on a fourth, and the progress announcement in a press meeting covered by the newspapers. All of it public. Almost none of it findable.
why.p2: Andhra Pradesh Fact Check does one thing: it gathers what the government has already published into a single place and organises it — by project, by district, by department — so that anyone can follow the work being done in their name without needing to know which of a dozen portals to search.
why.p3: We create nothing. We add nothing. We show existing public records, link every one back to where the government published it, and make it accessible to everyone — in English and in Telugu, free, with no login.

linksHome.body: Every project, tender, MoU, and document on this platform carries a link to the government page it came from and the date we collected it. If you cannot trace a number back to its source in two clicks, we consider that our bug.

dated.title: Dated, not "current"

noSide.title: No side to take
noSide.body: The platform tracks work, not parties. The same project keeps its page and its history through every change of government. What was promised, what was sanctioned, what was built — the record speaks for itself.

disclaimer.title: Disclaimer
disclaimer.lead: The short version: we are an independent citizen platform mirroring public government records, with a source link and timestamp on everything — and if something here is wrong, we fix it within 48 hours of being told.

whoWeAre.title: Who we are — and who we are not
whoWeAre.p1: Andhra Pradesh Fact Check is an independent, non-governmental transparency platform built and maintained by private citizens. We are NOT affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to the Government of Andhra Pradesh, the Government of India, any government department, or any political party.
whoWeAre.p2: This website is not an official government website. Nothing here constitutes an official government communication. For official information, always refer to the government portals we link to.

dataSources.title: Where our data comes from
dataSources.p1: Every data point on this platform is collected from publicly accessible official sources: the AP e-Procurement portal, the Government Orders Issue Register (GOIR), the AP Finance Department, CAG audit reports, the Open Government Data platform, the AP Economic Development Board, Press Information Bureau releases, and published news reports.
dataSources.p2: We do not create, estimate, or modify any figure. Progress percentages are the government's own announced figures. Documents are the government's own published files. Where no official figure exists, we display none.
dataSources.p3: Every item shows its source with a link to the original government page and the date and time we last collected it. The "Sources" list on our About page is the complete register of where this platform draws from.

accuracy.title: Accuracy and timeliness
accuracy.p1: We display data as published by the original sources at the time of collection. Government portals update, correct, and remove information without notice, so what appears here may lag behind the official source.
accuracy.p2: Always verify against the linked original source before acting on any information found here. This platform is provided for general public awareness only. It is not legal, financial, investment, or professional advice, and it is not an official record.
accuracy.p3: A tender shown as open may have closed; a progress figure may have been superseded; a document may have been revised. The "last synced" timestamp on each item tells you exactly how current our copy is.

copyright.title: Copyright and content
copyright.p1: Government Orders, Acts, notifications, reports, and similar public records are reproduced in accordance with the exemptions provided under Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957, which permits the reproduction of government works of this nature.
copyright.p2: News content: we display only headlines, source attributions, and short AI-generated summaries clearly labeled as such. Full articles remain on the publishers' websites, and every headline links to the original publisher. We do not host or republish full news articles.
copyright.p3: Documents in our library link to the original file on the government portal wherever possible. Where we hold a cached copy for reliability, the original source link is always displayed alongside it, together with the date of retrieval.

ai.title: AI-generated summaries
ai.p1: Summaries marked "AI Summary" are generated automatically to make long articles and documents easier to scan. They may contain errors and are not a substitute for the original text. The original is always linked — read it before relying on any detail.

corrections.title: Corrections and takedown requests
corrections.p1: If you believe any information displayed here is inaccurate, outdated, defamatory, or should not be displayed, write to us with a link to the specific item. We review every request within 48 hours and will correct, update, annotate, or remove content where warranted — and note that we did so.
corrections.p2: This applies to everyone: citizens, officials, contractors, and companies named in public records alike. We show public records as published; if the record itself is wrong, we will link to any official correction once one is published.

branding.title: Emblems and official marks
branding.p1: This platform deliberately does not use the State Emblem of Andhra Pradesh, the State Emblem of India, or any official government seal, logo, or insignia — their use by private entities is restricted under the State Emblem of India (Prohibition of Improper Use) Act, 2005, and using them would wrongly suggest official status. Our logo and branding are original marks.

liability.title: Limitation of liability
liability.p1: To the maximum extent permitted by law, Andhra Pradesh Fact Check and its maintainers accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from the use of, or reliance on, information displayed on this platform. Use of this platform is at your own discretion, and the linked official sources remain the authoritative record in every case.

withdrawn.title: The spending comparison has been withdrawn
withdrawn.body: This section carried a comparison of money sanctioned by each government. It has been removed because the extraction behind it was wrong in a way that was **not neutral**: it read amounts written as "Rs.9,37,63,92,000/-" but silently skipped amounts written as "Rs.944.53 crores". That dropped about **₹28,019 crore of YSRCP orders against ₹955 crore of TDP 2014-19 orders** — so the chart showed one government ahead when the missing money points the other way. Two further problems: sanction orders, budget releases and instalments of the same scheme each state a figure, so adding them counts the same rupee more than once; and the total mixed school construction with pension arrears, exam costs and private-school administration. It will return only when the extraction is rebuilt and checked against the Demands for Grants capital outlay series, not merely against itself. **Order counts below are exact and unaffected.**

limits.title: What this page can and cannot answer
limits.canBody: How much was budgeted for school education each year since 2014-15, how much was revised, and what the audited accounts finally recorded — including how much of it was capital outlay. And, from the state’s own ten-year table, how many schools were government-run, aided or private in each year, with the students and teachers in each.
limits.cannotBody: Why a count changed. The state publishes the numbers but not the reasons, so a fall can be a closure, a merger of two schools into one, or a change in what was counted — and this page will not guess between them. The clearest case is 2015-16, when local-body schools drop by 1,752 in a single year with no explanation given. Enrolment before 2016-17 also sits on a wider definition and is not comparable with what follows.
